best-literary-magazines-to-submit-to.body:
> [!NOTE]
> The groups in this guide are reading routes we chose to help you start. They aren’t official tiers, acceptance predictions or Missa’s numbered rankings.

## What makes a literary magazine “top tier”?

Usually a mix of prize recognition, readership, pay and editorial history, and each of those measures something different.

Prize anthologies show which published pieces other editors picked. Contributor pay tells you about the terms writers get. Readership is about who might come across your work. None of them makes one magazine the best home for every manuscript.

So pick the measure first. If you want readers of short literary fiction, a magazine built around that form may matter more than a bigger name. If you’ve written a short personal essay, find a journal that publishes those. Don’t push it through a fiction category because the title looks impressive.

Tiers help when they make those choices visible. They mislead when they squash everything into one label. A journal can pay well and reply slowly, publish excellent work to a small readership, or be exactly right for one community.

## How do literary magazine rankings work?

Each ranking counts something different, so read its method before you use its order to choose where to submit.

[Clifford Garstang’s 2026 overview](https://cliffordgarstang.com/2026-literary-magazine-rankings-overview/) ranks magazines by Pushcart Prizes and Special Mentions over a rolling ten years, with recent recognition counting more, and keeps fiction, nonfiction and poetry separate. It doesn’t count submission fees, contributor pay or response time, and it leaves out commercial magazines such as The New Yorker and Harper’s.

That makes it a good measure of one kind of recognition. It doesn’t make the top journal the cheapest, the easiest to reach or the right place for your story.

[Missa’s ranking method](/rankings/methodology) scores each magazine out of 100 across six measures: honors, pay, reply time, fees, submission policy, and archive and ethics. Honors, mainly Pushcart recognition, carry the most weight, at up to 40 points. A fact nobody has recorded earns half its points, so part of a score can reflect what’s missing. Look at the record behind any score. This describes the published method; it isn’t an outside audit of the data.

| Missa tier | Score | How to use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tier 1: Flagship Luminary | 75 and above | Check the evidence behind a high score |
| Tier 2: High Distinction | 60–74.9 | Compare fit and terms within the group |
| Tier 3: Distinguished Contemporary | 45–59.9 | Look past the label to the work |
| Tier 4: Emerging & Community | Below 45 | See which facts are missing before you judge |

These are Missa’s current score bands, not universal literary tiers. The [full magazine rankings](/rankings/magazines) show where each magazine sits.

Acceptance rates are a separate thing. Missa doesn’t publish them, and they aren’t one of the six measures. A low reported rate is no substitute for reading the magazine, and it doesn’t earn a place in a reputation ranking. Our [acceptance-rate guide](/guides/literary-magazine-acceptance-rates) explains the difference.

## Which literary magazines should you research first?

Start with a small set that suits your work, and read them before you add more.

The examples below are grouped by what you might want from a submission, not by quality. Being on the list doesn’t mean every category is open today, so check each magazine’s current route. Use it to start reading, not to open forty new tabs.

| Reading route | Magazine | Why it’s on the list | Ask before you send |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Widely recognized | [The New Yorker](https://www.newyorker.com/about/contact) | Read the fiction or poetry it actually runs | Is your genre’s route open? Fiction’s route is changing in 2026 |
| Widely recognized | [The Paris Review](https://www.theparisreview.org/about/submissions) | Prose and poetry, with a route for unsolicited work | Which online month applies, and is the cap reached? |
| Widely recognized | [Poetry](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/submit) | Poetry only; free to submit, with published pay rates | Is it open, and can you wait as long as it says? |
| Long-standing journals | [Ploughshares](https://pshares.org/product/manuscript-submission/) | Fiction, poetry and nonfiction, each with its own terms | Are you sending to the journal or its separate contest? |
| Long-standing journals | [The Kenyon Review](https://kenyonreview.org/submit/) | Several forms; no general reading fee stated | When’s the next window? September 2026’s has closed |
| Long-standing journals | [AGNI](https://agnionline.bu.edu/submit/) | Poetry, prose and hybrid work; explains how it reads | Does the work fit, and which route will you use? |
| Form or mission first | [One Story](https://one-story.com/write/submit-a-story/) | Built around the standalone literary short story | Is it 3,000–8,000 words, and is it reading now? |
| Form or mission first | [Brevity](https://brevitymag.com/submissions/) | Essays of 750 words or fewer | Is it a complete short essay, not an excerpt? |
| Form or mission first | [A Public Space](https://apublicspace.org/about/resources) | Several genres, and work that crosses them | Which current call fits your form? |
| Form or mission first | [The Common](https://www.thecommononline.org/submit/) | Work with a strong sense of place | Is place essential to the piece? Which category? |
| Form or mission first | [The Sun](https://www.thesunmagazine.org/submit) | Personal essays, fiction, poetry and photography | General rules, or the separate Readers Write rules? |

Pick a few, read their current work and note why your piece belongs there. If another journal is a better match, swap out the famous name.

## What are the best magazines for poetry, fiction and essays?

The best ones for you publish the form and length you’ve written, so match those first and weigh reputation after.

### Poetry

Start with magazines whose recent poems show interest in the forms you write. Poetry, The Paris Review, Ploughshares, The Kenyon Review and AGNI each read differently, and their names aren’t interchangeable. Read a run of poems from a recent issue, so one poem doesn’t become your whole picture of the magazine.

Notice range, length, how the poems use the page and how a group of poems hangs together. Send a coherent set of your strongest eligible poems. Don’t pad a packet with weaker work to reach the maximum.

The [Poetry submission page](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/submit) says submitting is free and lists current pay rates. The [Paris Review guidelines](https://www.theparisreview.org/about/submissions) set separate online months for poetry and take postal submissions all year. Details like these shape your schedule as much as reputation does.

For a wider search, browse [poetry calls](/discover/poetry) and check whether each result is a magazine, contest, residency or grant. Each asks you for a different decision, even under the same poetry label.

### Fiction

Match the story’s length and form before you rank anything by reputation. [One Story](https://one-story.com/write/submit-a-story/) asks for literary stories of 3,000 to 8,000 words, so a flash piece isn’t a fit for its general submissions, however good it is.

For broader literary fiction, read The Paris Review, Ploughshares, AGNI, The Kenyon Review and A Public Space, then find the real matches. Check whether they take excerpts, translations or work with genre elements, and go by the magazine’s own wording, not a directory label.

Routes change. The New Yorker’s [contact page](https://www.newyorker.com/about/contact) says its fiction email route closed in August 2026 and that fiction reopens through Submittable on November 1, 2026. An older article telling you to email your story is out of date. Check each route right before you send, even when the manuscript’s ready.

Search [fiction calls](/discover/fiction) for what’s open now, and keep a note of places to revisit when their next window opens.

### Essays

Know what kind of essay you have before you choose: personal, flash, criticism, a dispatch or reported work.

Brevity takes essays of 750 words or fewer. The Sun publishes personal essays alongside other forms. The Common cares about place and has separate guidance for dispatches. A Public Space welcomes essays and work that doesn’t fit a genre label.

Read the right section. A review, interview or editorial essay in an issue doesn’t mean the magazine takes unsolicited work in that form. Some sections are commissioned or need a pitch.

Check whether the piece has been online before. Some guidelines count a post on a personal website or social account as already published, whether or not you were paid for it.

Use [creative nonfiction calls](/discover/creative-nonfiction) to widen the search, then narrow by form and length. One clear match beats a long list of magazines that publish “nonfiction” in some form.

## Which literary magazines pay writers?

Several well-known magazines publish their rates: [Poetry](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/submit) lists US$500 per text poem from its March 2026 issue, [One Story](https://one-story.com/write/submit-a-story/) lists US$500 per accepted story, and [Brevity](https://brevitymag.com/submissions/) lists a US$45 honorarium for featured essays.

Those are published examples, not rates for every category, and an individual contract can differ.

Paying and charging are separate questions. A paying magazine may still charge a submission fee, and a free one may still pay. Read our [guide to submission fees and tip jars](/guides/literary-magazine-submission-fees) before you spend money.

Before you accept, read the contract: rights, exclusivity, when you’re paid and contributor copies. A high ranking doesn’t settle whether those terms work for you. If something’s unclear, ask the editor before you agree.

## How should you order submissions across tiers?

By fit, the practical rules and your goals, with reputation as one factor among them.

If several good matches allow simultaneous submissions, send to a first group at once instead of waiting on each in turn. Check each policy, log every destination and withdraw quickly if the piece is taken elsewhere.

If a magazine wants exclusive consideration, decide whether the wait is worth it. You might keep one piece for that magazine and send other work where simultaneous submissions are fine. Don’t break an exclusivity rule to speed things up.

A good shortlist has some ambitious picks, some long-standing journals that fit well and some smaller magazines you value. The groups don’t need to be the same size. Keep the list small enough that you can track every reading period and withdrawal rule.

Look again as decisions arrive. A rejection on its own isn’t an instruction to revise, and a personal note isn’t a contract. Revise when you have a clear editorial reason, and keep track of which version each magazine has.

## Are newer online magazines worth submitting to?

Yes, when the work they publish and their terms meet your standards.

A newer magazine may have little prize history and too few tracker reports for useful statistics. Read what it has published, find out who the editors are and check that its submission terms are clear. A short record is a reason to look closely, not to rule it out.

Look at how it presents contributors, whether back issues stay online and how it explains rights and fees. If you want to reach a particular community or try a form, a smaller online magazine can be a strong choice.

Print isn’t a stand-in for quality. A stable online archive, careful editing and readers who care about your work can matter more than a printed contributor copy.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is there an official literary magazine tier list?

No. Each ranking follows its own method or one editor’s judgment, so read the criteria before you use it.

### Should I always submit to the most famous magazine first?

Only if the work fits and you’re fine with its rules, costs and wait. Reputation doesn’t make up for the wrong genre or length.

### Can a newer magazine be the best place for my work?

Yes. Read what it publishes and check its editing and terms. A strong match can matter more than a long prize record.

### How does Missa rank literary magazines?

Out of 100, across six measures. Honors, mainly Pushcart recognition, are worth up to 40 points. A missing fact earns half its points, and scores fall into four tiers. The [method page](/rankings/methodology) explains each measure.

duotrope-alternatives.body:
> [!NOTE]
> Missa publishes this guide and is in the comparison. We checked each tool’s own pages on October 7, 2026. Prices are what writers pay for the tool; any magazine’s submission fee is extra.

A good tracker answers three questions without a trip through your inbox: what did you send, who has it, and what needs doing next? A market database does a different job. It helps you pick where to send. Some tools do both, and you don’t have to buy both in one subscription.

## What does Duotrope do best?

Duotrope’s strength is research: a searchable database of publishers and agents, editor interviews, and response and acceptance statistics built from its users’ reports, all sitting next to a submission tracker.

Its [subscription FAQ](https://duotrope.com/about/payment.aspx) lists a one-time 10-day trial, then US$6 a month or US$60 a year. Twelve monthly payments come to US$72, so paying yearly saves US$12. Check the price in your currency at checkout.

Pay for it if you use the research. If you check a magazine’s reported response time before every submission, compare similar markets and lean on the detailed search, the subscription can save you hours. If you send a few pieces a year, free tools and reading the magazines yourself may be enough.

Read the numbers the way Duotrope asks you to. Its [statistics page](https://duotrope.com/about/statistics.aspx) separates figures from user reports from figures for a whole publication. Response data helps you plan the wait and the follow-up. It can’t promise a decision date, and no percentage can tell you how an editor will read your next story.

Before you cancel, list the Duotrope features you actually use. Swapping one subscription for three free tools isn’t a win if you end up doing more admin.

## Is there a free alternative to Duotrope?

Yes. The Submission Grinder is free and donation-based, Chill Subs has a free basic tracker, and a free Submittable account can log work you sent elsewhere.

A spreadsheet works too, if you keep it current. Whatever you try, test it with a few real records: one rejection, one piece still out, and one accepted somewhere else.

“Docs don’t say” below means the tool’s own help pages didn’t mention the feature when we checked. It may still exist.

| Tool | Price | Finding markets | Your own tracking | Response and acceptance data | Deadline reminders | Spreadsheet import |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Duotrope](https://duotrope.com/about/payment.aspx) | US$6/month or US$60/year after a 10-day trial | Publisher and agent database | Yes | From its users’ reports | Theme and deadline calendar; reminder emails: docs don’t say | Docs don’t say |
| [Submission Grinder](https://thegrinder.diabolicalplots.com/Home/FAQ) | Free; donation-based | Writing-market search | Yes | Pooled anonymous reports from users | Docs don’t say | Docs don’t say |
| [Chill Subs](https://support.chillsubs.com/how-tos/how-to-use-our-submission-tracker) | Basic tracker free; [Better US$10/month](https://support.chillsubs.com/faq/memberships) | Literary magazine listings | Yes, in table or board view | Community-reported, plus some figures labeled official | Calendar; reminder emails: docs don’t say | Your own CSV, Submittable or Grinder |
| [Submittable](https://submittable.help/en/articles/8048419-manage-my-submissions) | Free account for applicants | Discover page | Yes, including work you log from elsewhere | No market-wide statistics in its docs | Docs don’t say | CSV export; import: docs don’t say |
| Spreadsheet | Free if you already have the software | Your own research | By hand | Your own records only | Set calendar reminders yourself | It’s already your file |
| Missa | Finding calls, saving them and email reminders are free | Art, writing, film, music and performance calls | Yes | No acceptance rates | Two weeks, one week, three days and one day before | CSV import at [/import](/import) |

Missa’s row is about calls and tracking. For magazine research it has [journal profiles](/journals) and [magazine rankings](/rankings/magazines), but no acceptance rates. Our [acceptance-rate guide](/guides/literary-magazine-acceptance-rates) explains why those numbers need care wherever you find them.

## Submission Grinder vs. Duotrope: which should you choose?

Choose The Submission Grinder if its market search and tracking cover the magazines you send to and a subscription isn’t in your budget.

The Grinder’s [FAQ](https://thegrinder.diabolicalplots.com/Home/FAQ) calls the site donation-based, funded by writers’ donations and monthly sponsorships, and says the team would rather close it than charge for access. You don’t need a paid membership to log work. If an older review calls it ad-supported, the FAQ tells a different story.

Test its coverage against the magazines you already read. Search for one you send to now, one you barely know and one that’s closed. Then open each magazine’s own guidelines for the fee, who can submit and whether it’s reading now.

For your own records, use the same title for each piece every time and note the version. Log every decision, the dull ones included. If writers report only acceptances, or only rejections, the shared statistics skew. Keep work that’s still out separate from work that never got a reply, and follow each magazine’s rules on queries.

Duotrope may suit you better if you use its search, interviews or agent research every week. The Grinder may suit you better if free access and a plain record are enough. Log a week of real submissions in each before you decide.

## Chill Subs vs. Duotrope: what’s different?

Chill Subs is worth a look if you want literary magazine listings, a free basic tracker and an easy way to bring your old records with you.

Its [tracker guide](https://support.chillsubs.com/how-tos/how-to-use-our-submission-tracker) covers table and board views, custom entries for publishers it doesn’t list, notes, CSV export and three import routes: from Submittable, from the Grinder or from your own CSV. That’s a real head start if you’re leaving a spreadsheet.

The paid tier, Chill Subs Better, is US$10 a month, according to the [membership FAQ](https://support.chillsubs.com/faq/memberships), and adds website tools such as keyword search and a prose formatter. Sub Club, a newsletter, and Forever Workshop, a monthly writing workshop, are separate memberships. Check which one includes the tool you want before you pay.

If you use its statistics, check where each number comes from. The [listing guide](https://support.chillsubs.com/how-tos/how-to-navigate-our-listing-pages) says an asterisk marks community-sourced figures, and an “Editor’s Report” section shows figures it labels official. Both can sit on the same page, so read the label before you repeat a number.

Import a few rows before you move everything, and check which publisher each one matched. An upload that works isn’t the same as a history that mapped correctly.

## Can Submittable track submissions you sent elsewhere?

Yes. Submittable’s external submissions tool lets you log work you sent without Submittable, by hand.

Some older comparisons say it can’t, so this one’s worth correcting. The [external submissions guide](https://submittable.help/en/articles/13380905-external-submissions) walks through adding one: choose Add External Submission, enter the organization, pick a status and fill in the required fields. The [My Submissions guide](https://submittable.help/en/articles/8048419-manage-my-submissions) also lets you download the submissions on screen as a CSV.

If most of the magazines you send to already use Submittable, external entries might make it enough as your main tracker. Test it with an email submission and one sent through another organizer’s form. Then check you can tell those manual entries apart from submissions the receiving organization updates.

What it won’t do is update itself. An external entry isn’t connected to the other service, so you change the status when a decision arrives. It also doesn’t give you the market-wide response research of a dedicated database. If you want that, pair a directory with your own record.

## Should you just use a spreadsheet?

Use a spreadsheet if you mostly want a dependable record and you’re happy to keep the dates, statuses and reminders yourself.

Start small. Give each submission its own row, and don’t overwrite the last destination when a piece comes back. If several versions share a title, give each one an ID.

| Column | What to record | Why it helps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Work and version | Title plus an ID you’ll recognize | Stops you sending an old draft |
| Publication or organizer | Name and official guidelines URL | Makes the next rule check quick |
| Category | Fiction, poetry, essay, grant or residency | Keeps different rules apart |
| Submitted date | A date nobody can misread | Keeps your waiting records accurate |
| Deadline and time zone | For planned applications | Gives your calendar the right cutoff |
| Status | Planned, sent, accepted, rejected or withdrawn | Shows what still needs action |
| Response date | When the decision actually came | Builds your own response history |
| Fee and currency | What you actually paid | Lets you review what you spend |
| Notes | Withdrawals, queries and rights | Keeps context a status can’t hold |

The weak spot is upkeep. Set a short weekly review and log acceptances the day they arrive. Your calendar won’t remind you of anything unless you’ve set it up and checked it works, and a formula that counts days doesn’t send an email.

Don’t mark a quiet magazine as a rejection. Keep the piece pending until the guidelines or an actual decision say otherwise.

## How do you move your submission history out of a spreadsheet?

Back up the original, clean a copy, and test the importer with a handful of rows before you bring the rest. Yes, even the color-coded one.

Missa is one place to bring it, especially if you also apply for residencies, grants, prizes or art, film, music and performance calls. The tracker keeps what you sent, where and when, and saved calls get an email two weeks, one week, three days and one day before the deadline, in your time zone. You still apply on each organizer’s page, not through Missa, so keep their receipt or confirmation email with your records. For finding calls beyond magazines, see [where to find open calls](/guides/where-to-find-open-calls).

The move itself, in any tracker:

1. Keep the original file untouched and work in a copy.
2. Make your status labels consistent and your dates unambiguous.
3. Map the columns. [Missa’s importer](/import) maps title, organization and status, plus optional deadline, submitted date, response date, work, genre, fee, notes and source URL. Use “title” for the call or submission and “work” for the poem, story or artwork, if your sheet keeps them apart.
4. Import the hard cases first: a multi-poem packet, a partial withdrawal, a magazine that has closed, and two records with similar names. If a detail has no column of its own, put it in notes and keep it in your backup.
5. Review the rows before you confirm. Missa’s importer has a review step for this.
6. Compare the record totals, then open a pending piece, an acceptance and an old rejection.
7. Set reminders only once you’ve checked that deadlines and time zones came through correctly. Keep the old system until you’ve fixed any mismatches.

> [!TIP]
> Write dates as year-month-day, like 2026-03-04, if the importer accepts it. A date like 03/04/2026 can mean March 4 or April 3, depending on who wrote it.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is The Submission Grinder still free?

Yes. Its [FAQ](https://thegrinder.diabolicalplots.com/Home/FAQ) calls it donation-based and says the team would rather close the site than charge for access. Check the page itself before you trust an older review.

### Do I need Duotrope to submit through Duosuma?

No. [Duosuma’s information for writers](https://duotrope.com/duosuma/info-for-submitters.aspx) treats sending work through Duosuma and subscribing to Duotrope as separate things. A magazine can still charge its own submission fee.

### Will a tracker withdraw my work from other magazines?

Don’t count on it. Follow each magazine’s withdrawal rules, then update your tracker. Logging an acceptance doesn’t tell the other editors.

### What’s the best free submission tracker?

The one you’ll keep up to date. Test imports, exports, status changes and reminders with a few records before you move your whole history.

meta.answer: An entry fee pays for your work to be considered. A hanging fee pays to show selected work. A participation fee covers taking part once you’re selected. entry-fees-hanging-fees-participation-fe.body:
## What’s the difference between an entry fee and a hanging fee?

You pay an entry fee before selection, to have your work considered. You pay a hanging fee after selection, to have it shown.

An entry fee also goes by jury fee, submission fee or administration charge. It buys consideration, not a place in the show. If your work isn’t picked, the rules often say the fee isn’t refundable.

A hanging fee pays for showing selected work, per artwork, per wall or per exhibition. A participation fee is broader and might cover installation, publicity or an opening. The labels promise nothing on their own, so check the written agreement for what the organizer provides.

Here are the charges to look for. The Royal Academy figure is one real example, not a market rate. “Varies” means we couldn’t find a reliable general range, so ask the organizer for the number.

| Cost | When you pay | How it’s charged | Fair when | Pause when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Entry or jury fee | Before selection | Per work or entry. [Royal Academy 2026](https://summer.royalacademy.org.uk/Home/): £40 a work | Selection process and rules are clear | No named organizer or judging process |
| Extra artwork fee | When you enter more work | Varies by number of works or category | You know the total before you submit | New charges appear at checkout |
| Hanging or wall fee | Usually after selection | Varies: per artwork, wall or show | Space, dates and services are defined | “Selected” work needs a payment you weren’t told about |
| Participation fee | After selection or on confirmation | Varies | You get a written list of services you want | Pressure to buy a package to keep your place |
| Sales commission | After a sale | A percentage or fixed amount; varies | The basis, tax and payment date are clear | Nobody can explain what you’ll actually receive |
| Shipping and insurance | Before delivery and return | Depends on the quote | Who’s responsible and what’s covered is agreed | No return plan, or unclear liability for damage |
| Catalog or marketing package | Before production or participation | Varies; may be optional | Clear deliverables you’d want anyway | It becomes compulsory after “acceptance” |

## Is a participation fee after selection normal?

Some exhibitions do charge selected artists a participation fee, and that’s fine as long as the call says so before you apply.

> [!WARNING]
> If the acceptance email is the first place you see a charge, stop. Ask for the full terms in writing before you pay anything.

Ask what happens if you say no after being selected. Do you owe anything? Is the entry fee refunded if the show is canceled? Are installation, storage or return delivery charged separately? Keep the answers with the call’s terms.

A clear fee isn’t automatically good value. If it’s more than the show is worth to you, say no. That’s a budget decision, not an accusation.

[CaFÉ](https://www.callforentry.org/administrator-help-center/cafe-product-updates/) lets artists filter calls by entry fee and, separately, by participation fee. That’s a good reminder to check both, even when a call looks cheap in search results.

## How much is a normal art competition entry fee?

There’s no single “normal” entry fee that tells you whether a competition is fair.

Compare the actual fee with the selection process, the venue, the services, the published terms and your budget. A high fee doesn’t mean a better show. A low fee doesn’t mean a legitimate one.

The [Royal Academy’s 2026 Summer Exhibition](https://summer.royalacademy.org.uk/Home/), for example, charged £40 per artwork for one or two works. A digital round came first, and work that got through was delivered for further selection. That call has closed, and it shows one organizer’s model, not a recommended price.

Add up what the whole application really costs. Photographing work, preparing files, framing and time away from paid work can cost more than the entry fee. If you’re entering several works, check whether the fee covers all of them or just the first.

Set a personal limit: an amount you can spend even if nothing gets in. Pick it before you start browsing, and compare each paid call with the best free ones open to you. Don’t raise the limit because an organizer says the deadline is nearly here.

## Are pay-to-play galleries worth it?

A paid show is worth it only if you can name what you’re buying and judge its value for yourself.

Renting display space isn’t the same as a gallery taking you on. When you pay to show, you might be buying wall space, an event or promotion. Check the venue, dates, opening hours, who can visit and who handles sales, and ask for evidence of past shows, not a promise of exposure.

Be wary of claims that showing in a famous city will boost your career. The venue, the curatorial context and the actual audience matter more than the city in the email’s subject line. Photos of an installation don’t tell you who came or what sold.

Compare the offer with renting a local room, joining an artist cooperative or putting on a small show yourself. If you want to meet curators, ask which curators came to earlier shows and how the organizer knows. If you want to sell, ask how sales are handled and when artists get paid.

For warning signs in paid invitations, read [how to spot a scam open call or a vanity gallery](/guides/open-call-scams-vanity-galleries).

## What should “free” mean on an open call listing?

“Free to apply” should mean the application costs nothing. It doesn’t promise that every later cost is covered.

Four different things can look like “free”:

- **No application fee:** you can submit without paying to enter.
- **No participation fee:** the organizer doesn’t charge you to take part.
- **Funded participation:** someone else pays for specific costs.
- **No fee information:** the page doesn’t say.

A page that doesn’t mention a fee hasn’t confirmed there isn’t one. Read the application form and any linked conditions. The checkout page can turn up a required membership or another compulsory payment.

Missa’s cards show the fee, “No fee,” or “Fee not listed” when the organizer’s page doesn’t say. Our [methodology](/methodology) explains that gaps are shown, not quietly filled in. Treat the label as a starting point for the application cost, then check for charges after selection on the organizer’s page. The [guide to no-fee calls](/guides/no-fee-submission-opportunities) explains the same difference when you browse.

## How do I find every cost before I apply?

Read the call, the application form and the exhibition terms together, then ask in writing about any cost that’s missing.

Search them, attachments and FAQs included, for “fee,” “participation,” “commission,” “shipping,” “insurance,” “catalog,” “storage” and “return.” Save a copy of the terms you applied under.

Find each of these before you apply:

- [ ] Entry or jury fee, and whether it covers every work
- [ ] Fees for extra works or categories
- [ ] Hanging, wall or participation fee after selection
- [ ] Sales commission, and what it’s calculated on
- [ ] Shipping and insurance, both ways
- [ ] Framing, packing and installation
- [ ] Catalog, marketing or membership charges
- [ ] Storage charges
- [ ] Refund terms if you withdraw or the show is canceled
- [ ] Your own travel and accommodation

Then budget for two outcomes. If you’re rejected, you’re usually out the application and preparation costs. If you’re accepted, add delivery, framing, attending the show, accommodation and return shipping. Neither budget should count on a sale.

Here’s a made-up example, not a real organizer. An exhibition is free to enter but charges selected artists a £50 participation fee. Add £80 for shipping there and back and £40 for packing materials. If you’re accepted, that’s £170 before framing or travel. “Free entry” was true about the first step and incomplete about the decision.

If there’s sales commission, ask what the percentage is calculated on and whether tax or transaction charges come off separately. The organizer should be able to show you a worked example using an artwork price. Don’t borrow another gallery’s commission formula for your own budget.

> [!TIP]
> When a cost is missing, send this before you apply: “Please confirm every required charge for applicants and selected artists, including exhibition, installation, catalog, sales, storage and return costs, and send your cancellation and refund terms.”

## How should I decide whether to pay?

Pay only when a call passes three checks: you’re eligible, you can name what you’re getting, and you can afford the full cost.

1. Check that your work meets the requirements.
2. Name a specific benefit: a juried show that suits the work, a defined audience, a prize, or services you’d otherwise pay for.
3. Check that you can absorb the total cost if nothing sells and no further invitation comes.

A fee isn’t an investment with a predictable return. A show can be worth it for reasons other than sales, but the reason should be yours. Write it down before you pay. “Show this series in a venue whose program fits it” is clearer than “get exposure.”

If the charge is more than you can spend, look at [free contests](/discover/free-contests), [no-fee calls](/discover/no-fee-calls), local programs or fee waivers. Writers have a separate [guide to reading fees and tip jars](/guides/literary-magazine-submission-fees), where the costs work differently.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does a jury fee guarantee my work will be shown?

No. A jury fee usually pays for consideration only. Read the selection and refund terms before you enter.

### Is a hanging fee the same as sales commission?

No. A hanging fee pays for display. Commission is usually taken when work sells, under the agreement. A show can charge both.

### Can a free-entry exhibition still be expensive?

Yes. Participation, packing, framing, shipping, insurance and travel can all still be on you. Work out your budget for being accepted before you apply.

### What if the organizer won’t tell me the full cost?

Hold off on applying. You can’t judge value or affordability without the terms, so keep the fee marked as unknown until they answer.

free-artist-residencies.body:
## Are there artist residencies with no application fee?

Yes. Some residencies take applications for free, but check the current cycle's rules every time.

The [Edward F. Albee Foundation](https://apply.albeefoundation.org/) is a clear example: its application page says there's no fee of any kind, from application through residency. Its next window for writers and visual artists runs January 11 to February 15, 2027, so it's a model to know, not a call you can enter today.

A fee waiver is a different route, and you have to qualify or ask before you pay. MacDowell charges no residency fee but a [US$30 processing fee](https://www.macdowell.org/apply/application-guidelines) to apply, and you can request a hardship waiver after you start the application and before you submit it. Don't assume a waiver from a past cycle still applies.

Start with [residencies with no application fee](/discover/residencies-no-fee), then open the organizer's page. Look for a plain zero on the form itself, and check for any required membership. Missa cards show the fee, "No fee", or "Fee not listed" when the organizer's page doesn't say. Treat "not listed" as unknown until you get an answer.

## What does "fully funded" usually cover?

"Fully funded" means the organizer pays for a stated package, and only that program's written terms tell you what's in it.

Turn the phrase into an itemized budget. Housing, a studio and meals help, but they don't mean your flights, materials or bills at home are paid. A cash stipend might cover living costs, might have rent taken out, or might arrive only after you get there.

[RESONANCE](https://www.artxlagos.com/resonance) shows the gap. Its closed 2026–2027 call described a three-month Paris residency with a live-in studio, a monthly allowance and travel to Paris. The visa and insurance stayed with the artist. A strong package can still need money upfront.

Use the table to turn each line into a question for the organizer:

| Budget item | What "covered" should mean | What to ask |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Application | Nothing to pay to enter, or a confirmed waiver | Is there a charge on the form, or a required membership? |
| Housing | Somewhere to live for the whole required stay | Are utilities, deposits and arrival nights included? |
| Studio | Suitable space you can actually use | Is equipment included? Are there usage charges? |
| Stipend | An amount, a currency and a payment date | Is rent deducted? When does the first payment reach me? |
| Travel | Named trips, with any spending cap | Do you book tickets, or pay me back afterward? |
| Visa and permits | Named fees paid, or real help with documents | Who pays the fees and supplies the paperwork? |
| Meals | A set meal plan or allowance | Which days and meals are covered? |
| Materials | A production budget you can use | What counts, and do I need approval first? |
| Access and family needs | An arrangement that meets your needs | Can you support an assistant, dependents or accessible housing? |

## What costs can a free residency leave out?

A residency with no attendance fee can still leave you paying for travel, materials, insurance, family costs and lost income.

List the cost of saying yes next to the support on offer, including the bills at home that keep running while you're away. A residency can give you a bedroom and still be out of reach if you have to stop paid work with nothing to replace it.

Then check the order of payments. If travel is reimbursed at the end, you have to buy the ticket first. If the stipend starts days after you arrive, you need money for food and local transport until it lands. The Albee Foundation is a real case. Its US$2,500 stipend for domestic fellows is paid after the residency, and so is its expense reimbursement for international fellows, capped at US$2,500 and paid against proof of costs.

Here's the arithmetic with invented numbers, not a typical award. Say a residency offers a US$1,000 stipend. If travel costs US$600 and insurance and documents another US$150, you have US$250 left before materials or home bills. Do the same sum with the organizer's real figures.

When money crosses borders, ask about conversion and transfer charges, and budget from the organizer's payment terms, not an exchange rate you haven't checked. If a fixed travel grant might fall short, get a current fare quote before you decide you can go.

> [!WARNING]
> Ask when the money arrives, not just how much. A stipend or reimbursement paid after the stay won't pay for the ticket there.

## Do any residencies pay a stipend?

Yes, some do. A stipend is money paid to you, and it isn't the same thing as free housing or a free application.

Read the money section closely. Programs call it a living allowance, honorarium, bursary or grant. Find out how much you can actually use, what it's meant to cover, and what gets deducted.

[Jan van Eyck Academie](https://www.janvaneyck.nl/residency/apply) in Maastricht shows why. Its listed stipend is €1,500 a month, but rent for the studio apartment comes out of it, and there's a €2,750 enrollment fee. [MacDowell](https://www.macdowell.org/apply/financial-assistance) offers need-based stipends of up to US$1,500, set by the length of your stay, and you can only apply for one once you've been awarded a fellowship.

Don't assume everyone selected gets the same support. A scholarship might cut a fee instead of paying you cash, and a production budget might cover materials only, against receipts. If the terms mix several benefits, ask for a worked example: "this amount, minus this rent" is a different deal from housing plus a stipend you can spend freely.

For a wider shortlist, browse [current residency calls](/discover/residencies), then go back to each organizer's page for the actual package.

## What should I ask before I accept?

Before you say yes, get written answers to the questions that decide whether you can actually go.

- [ ] What exactly does the funding cover, item by item?
- [ ] How much is the stipend, in what currency, and when is the first payment?
- [ ] Is rent or anything else deducted from it?
- [ ] Do you book travel, or pay me back afterward? Is there a cap?
- [ ] Who pays for the visa, permits and insurance?
- [ ] Which meals are covered, and on which days?
- [ ] Is there a materials budget, and what does it cover?
- [ ] Can you meet my access needs, or support a child, partner or assistant?
- [ ] What happens if my visa is delayed or I need to move my dates?

## Are free residencies harder to get into?

You can't tell from the fee. A free application says nothing on its own about how selective a residency is.

A well-funded program may get a lot of applications, but who you're up against depends on its discipline, residence rules, selection criteria and number of places. A small local call and an international residency differ in far more than the fee.

Read the eligibility rules first, then ask whether your samples and proposal fit. A tough field calls for a balanced shortlist and strong materials, not for skipping a program because it's free or funded. Our [residency application guide](/guides/how-to-apply-artist-residency) covers samples, proposals and a preparation schedule.

## How do I search without mixing up free entry and funded attendance?

Filter for no application fee first. Then go back through your shortlist and read each program's money terms.

The first pass answers one question: can you enter without paying? The second records what support you'd get and what you'd still pay if selected. Give those separate columns, so a "free" label can't hide a stay you can't afford.

Check the application cycle and the residency dates together. A page might be taking applications for a stay more than a year away, and a program you like might be closed while it picks its residents. Keep closed programs as calendar research, not open calls.

On Missa, a no-fee residency result is where you start checking, not proof of a full funding package or visa eligibility. Every call links to the organizer's page, and you apply there. If you're based in Nigeria, the [Nigeria and Africa funding guide](/guides/fully-funded-opportunities-nigeria-africa) starts with eligibility.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is a free artist residency the same as a fully funded one?

No. "Free" may describe the application or the stay. "Fully funded" should come with an itemized list of what's covered and what isn't.

### Should I ask for a fee waiver before applying?

Yes, if the rules offer one and you need it. Check who qualifies and how to ask before you pay, and don't count on a refund later.

### Does a stipend cover travel?

Only if the terms say so. Travel can be separate, capped, reimbursed later or left to you, so confirm how it's paid before you book.

### Can I bring a child, partner or support person?

Sometimes. Jan van Eyck Academie, for one, lists a larger stipend and apartment for participants with children. Ask each program directly about housing, access and extra costs, because a general welcome isn't the same as permission or funding.

fully-funded-opportunities-nigeria-afric.body:
## What does "fully funded" mean on a call?

"Fully funded" means the organizer pays for a stated package. Your job is to find every cost inside that package and every cost outside it.

For a residency abroad, check travel, housing, workspace, meals, stipend, insurance and visa costs. For a grant, check what you can spend it on, when it's paid and what reports you'll owe. For a prize, separate the award from any travel or event support for shortlisted writers.

Funding and open status are two different facts. A program can fund generous residencies this year and have no open call today. A residency happening right now may have picked its people months ago.

Be careful with roundups that copy an old call. Follow the link to the organizer, find the current edition and open the actual form. An old "apply now" button or a search snippet isn't enough. Our [guide to no-fee and funded residencies](/guides/free-artist-residencies) shows how to turn a funding description into a real budget.

## Which programs should Nigerian artists and writers watch?

These four programs are worth knowing, but every cycle below was closed on October 7, 2026. Treat them as programs to watch for the next round, not calls to enter now.

Each one shows a different route to support, and a different eligibility lesson:

| Program | Who it was for | What it funded | Status on October 7, 2026 | What it teaches |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [G.A.S. Fellowship Award 2026](https://guestartistsspace.com/News/open-call-gas-fellowship-award-2026) | Nigerian artists, art writers and other named groups | Funded stays in Lagos and Ikise; terms vary by category | Closed; recipients announced | Each category has its own rules |
| [RESONANCE](https://www.artxlagos.com/resonance) | Visual artists, designers and curators living and working in Nigeria | Three months in Paris: live-in studio, allowance, travel | 2026–2027 window closed | Where you're based matters; any nationality can apply |
| [Prince Claus Seed Awards](https://princeclausfund.nl/faq) | People from, and living in, eligible countries | A cash award; check the permitted uses | 2026 cycle closed (deadline was January 8, 2026) | Origin and residence can both count |
| [Caine Prize for African Writing](https://www.caineprize.com/submissions) | Published short fiction by African writers | Prize money; check any event support | 2026 closed; next window not yet open | Publishers enter, not writers |

The Caine Prize's page says the next window opens in November 2026 and closes in January 2027, but its exact dates don't agree with each other. It lists "Monday, 21 November", and November 21, 2026 is a Saturday. Ask the prize to confirm before you plan around a date. For 2027, the page says the story must have been published between February 27, 2022 and February 27, 2026 and run 3,000 to 10,000 words.

## Are there funded calls in Nigeria itself?

Yes. Programs based in Nigeria can fund your work without the visa and long-haul flight a residency abroad needs.

The [G.A.S. Fellowship Award](https://guestartistsspace.com/News/open-call-gas-fellowship-award-2026), from Guest Artists Space Foundation and the Yinka Shonibare Foundation, is one, with separate categories and locations. Its [recipient announcement](https://guestartistsspace.com/News/Announcing-the-Recipients-of-the-GAS-Fellowship-Award-2026-for-Emerging-Nigerian-Artists-and-Mid-Career-Art-Writers) confirms the 2026 selection is done. Watch for the next edition instead of applying to this one.

The 2026 call shows what a funded package in naira can look like. The art writers' category listed a ₦1,900,000 stipend, travel and materials allowance, a ₦760,000 honorarium for running a three-day writing workshop, and a private room with a desk and en-suite bathroom in Lagos. Trips outside Lagos were at the resident's own cost, except to the G.A.S. Farm House.

Location inside Nigeria still matters. A residency in Lagos or Ikise can mean travel, time away from work and a temporary home. Check whether transport, meals and materials are paid, and whether you're expected to run workshops or public events.

Don't assume an art-writing category takes fiction or poetry. Art criticism, curatorial research and literary work can sit under different rules. Read the category definition and sample requirements before you choose. Strong work won't fix a mismatch between what you make and what the call wants.

## How do I check whether "international" includes Nigeria?

Check three things separately: your citizenship, where you live now and where you work. A call can restrict any of them, whether you're in Lagos, Accra or Dakar.

Read the whole eligibility paragraph, not just the word "international". A program might accept every nationality but require you to live in one country. Another might accept diaspora applicants but require a particular citizenship or family link. A regional grant might want both residence and a local project.

RESONANCE's [rules](https://www.artxlagos.com/resonance) require you to live and work in Nigeria, and accept any nationality within its categories. The Prince Claus Fund's [FAQ](https://princeclausfund.nl/faq) works differently: you must come from, and live and work in, an eligible country. The [Caine Prize](https://www.caineprize.com/submissions) counts you as an African writer if you're a national of an African country or have a parent who is African by birth or nationality. Those are three different tests.

Before you prepare any work, write down the answers:

| Question | What to write down |
| --- | --- |
| Citizenship or origin | The exact definition in the rules |
| Where you live | Where you must live when you apply and during the award |
| What you make | The kind of work accepted, not a broad label |
| Career stage | The organizer's definition and the proof it asks for |
| Availability | Dates, length and any in-person commitments |
| How to apply | Directly, by nomination, or through a publisher |

If a rule is unclear, email the organizer one short, factual question: "I'm a Nigerian citizen living and working in Abuja. Does the residence rule let me apply in the visual art category?" Include only what they need to answer it.

## What about visas and travel for residencies abroad?

Before you decide an overseas residency is affordable, find out who pays for travel and the visa, and when the money arrives.

Ask who books the flights, whether costs are capped, and whether the award pays before you leave or reimburses you after. Ask whether the organizer sends invitation documents and names a contact for travel. An invitation letter doesn't guarantee a visa.

Use the destination's official immigration site for the route that fits your actual activities and length of stay. The right permission can depend on paid work, public performances, teaching or other duties, as well as how long you'll stay. For France, start with the official [France-Visas service](https://france-visas.gouv.fr/en/) and the residency's own guidance. Another resident's visa route may not be yours.

Build your timeline from the organizer's confirmed dates and the visa process. Leave room for documents and delays, and don't treat a typical processing time as a promise. Ask what happens if your visa is delayed or refused, and whether the program can move your stay.

RESONANCE's closed call drew the line clearly: travel to Paris was covered, the visa and insurance weren't. Put both in your budget before you apply to a future edition.

## How do I pay entry fees in naira, or avoid them?

Start with calls that confirm no application fee. For any call that charges, check how you can pay and what the full charge will be.

Begin with [residencies with no application fee](/discover/residencies-no-fee) and [grants](/discover/grants). A grant isn't automatically free to apply for, and a no-fee residency isn't automatically funded to attend. Missa cards show the fee, "No fee", or "Fee not listed" when the organizer's page doesn't say.

If there's a fee, ask whether the organizer takes a payment method you can use and whether a waiver exists. Confirm the amount and currency at the actual checkout. Your bank or card provider can tell you its own conversion and transaction charges. Don't budget from an old exchange rate quoted in a roundup.

If a fee stands between you and a call that fits your work, a short waiver request is fine. Name the category, say you can't pay the application fee, and ask whether there's a waiver or another way to enter. You don't need to share your finances in the first message.

> [!WARNING]
> Pay only through the organizer's own payment page. If someone finds your public profile and offers to pay a fee for you, check with the organizer directly first, and never share a password or account access.

## How do I build a funding shortlist?

Keep two lists: calls you can enter now, and programs to watch. Otherwise a closed call can sit in an open tab for months, looking hopeful.

For each one, note the official source, the date you checked, your eligibility answer, what the funding covers, what you'd still pay and how you apply.

For each live call, set a preparation date and gather the samples. Our [residency application guide](/guides/how-to-apply-artist-residency) covers reusable materials and how to write the proposal. Fit the project to what the program actually offers, and don't claim partnerships or travel plans that aren't confirmed.

Missa's [country pages](/countries) help you find calls, but the organizer decides who's eligible. Check their current rules and apply on their page. Keep a copy of the call and your receipt, so you're not relying on memory if anything changes. Save a call on Missa and you'll get reminders two weeks, one week, three days and one day before the deadline, in your time zone.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can a Nigerian artist apply to an international residency?

Yes, when that program's nationality, residence, discipline and travel rules allow it. The word "international" on its own doesn't confirm it.

### Does fully funded include the visa fee?

Only if the funding terms say so. A program can cover travel and housing and still leave the visa and insurance to you.

### Can I apply directly to the Caine Prize?

No. Publishers enter eligible stories, with the writer's consent. Check the current edition and talk to your publisher about entering.

### Are G.A.S. and RESONANCE open now?

No. Both cycles cited here were closed on October 7, 2026. Watch each organizer for a new announcement.

how-to-apply-artist-residency.body:
## What does a residency application ask for?

Most residency applications ask for two things: proof of your work, and a clear account of how you'd use the time, space or support on offer.

The details belong to each program. A writer might send a manuscript excerpt, a visual artist an image sequence, a composer recordings and scores. Some programs want a detailed proposal; others care more about finished work.

Build one folder before you settle your shortlist: a current CV, a short bio, a longer statement, your strongest samples, captions and technical descriptions. Keep a clean master of each document and export copies for each application, so cutting a statement for one program never touches the original.

Then make a requirements sheet for each residency: file types, word and image counts, excerpt length, naming rules, and whether the panel sees your name. Good work can still fail on a wrong file or a private video link. Name each file the way the program asks. If it doesn't say, `Surname_Sample1.pdf` beats `final_FINAL_v3.pdf`.

Before you send anything, run through this:

- [ ] Check who can apply: career stage, degree status, where you live, past residents
- [ ] Find the application fee, any waiver, and what attending would cost you
- [ ] Note the deadline, its time zone and any cap on applications
- [ ] Read the file rules: types, counts, word limits, running times, file names
- [ ] Pick samples that support the proposal
- [ ] Write the proposal for this program's time, space and resources
- [ ] Ask for references only if the program wants them
- [ ] Open every link on another device, logged out
- [ ] Submit, then save the receipt

## When do the big residencies take applications?

Each residency runs its own calendar. As of October 7, 2026, Djerassi closes October 9 and Skowhegan October 16, Yaddo's winter window runs November 1 to December 20, Jan van Eyck closes December 1, and MacDowell and the Albee Foundation open their next windows in January 2027.

We checked every row on the program's own page on October 7, 2026. Deadlines move, so check again before you apply, and don't carry last year's date forward. The programs differ in kind, too: a studio residency, a retreat and a summer school ask different things of you, and a residency can be free to attend and still charge you to apply.

| Residency | Who it's for | Application window | Application fee | What you get | What to send |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Yaddo](https://yaddo.org/apply/) | Literature, visual art, music, performance, film and video | Winter window opens Nov 1; closes Dec 20, 2026 | US$35 | Room, board and studio; access grants can help you accept | Finished work in your discipline; no references needed now |

Albee Foundation](https://apply.albeefoundation.org/) | Writers and visual artists | Next window Jan 11–Feb 15, 2027 | No fee | Room, studio, and a stipend or capped reimbursement after the stay | [Samples by discipline](https://www.albeefoundation.org/guidelines--submitting.html) and a residency statement |

"Not listed" means the organizer's page doesn't say. Ask before you pay or plan around it.

> [!TIP]
> Write each deadline down in your own time zone. Skowhegan's 11:59 p.m. Eastern on October 16 is 4:59 a.m. on October 17 in London and Lagos.

## What do panels look for in a work sample?

Panels judge against each program's own criteria, and at MacDowell and Yaddo the work itself comes first. So a strong sample is your best eligible work that also backs up what you say you'll do there.

MacDowell says the [sole criterion](https://www.macdowell.org/apply/apply-for-fellowship) for acceptance is artistic excellence. Yaddo's [application page](https://yaddo.org/apply/) describes peer review and puts the weight on the quality of the work. Djerassi's [guidelines](https://djerassi.org/apply/application-guidelines/) describe panels of arts professionals in each category.

A famous referee won't rescue weak samples. And don't rule yourself out as too early in your career: check each program's career-stage, degree, past-resident and age rules. "Emerging" means different things in different places.

Then check that your samples hang together. A proposal about sound installations needs samples that show your decisions about sound, space or audience, not a spread picked to show range.

**Visual work.** Check exposure, scale and captions. Add installation views when the setting matters, and close details when they show something the full image can't. Give materials, dimensions and your part in any collaboration. Don't fill every slot with weaker pieces.

**Writing.** Pick an excerpt that stands on its own. If context is allowed, keep it short and factual, and get to the work fast. A long note about why the excerpt gets interesting later uses up time the sample needs.

**Film, performance and music.** If links are allowed, send one that opens without a login, and test the password and playback on another device. Point to the excerpt that matters and say what your role was. Stay inside the time limit. Sending the full recording ignores the format the panel asked for.

## How do I write a residency proposal?

A residency proposal says what you'll make or investigate, why this program suits it, and what you can realistically get done during the stay.

Answer four questions: what's the work, what stage is it at, what will you do there, and which of the program's resources matter? Keep the artistic question apart from the practical plan. You can leave the final outcome open and still be clear about the work you'll do.

Here's an invented outline that gives a panel something concrete:

*I'm developing a sequence of short essays about informal repair economies. During the residency I'll revise the finished opening essays and draft the next section, using interviews already recorded with participants' consent. The uninterrupted writing time and the program's library would support this stage. I expect to leave with a revised sequence and a plan for the remaining chapters.*

It's a structure to learn from, not text to copy. Write your own, and follow the program's rules on writing help. Add what's true for your project: permissions, equipment, and the limits of what you can finish.

Don't promise access you don't have. If the plan depends on an archive, a collaborator or a workshop, say whether that's confirmed, and give a fallback if it isn't. For a short stay, one focused phase of a longer project often reads clearer than a plan to finish everything.

## Do I need references, and when do I ask?

Only if the program asks for them. Check first whether it wants a letter or just contact details.

Yaddo currently says references aren't required. MacDowell has [temporarily suspended](https://www.macdowell.org/apply/application-guidelines) its reference letter requirement, and Skowhegan doesn't require letters of recommendation. Other programs may want a letter with the application or later in selection. Read the current instructions before you hand someone a deadline they don't need.

When you do need one, ask someone who knows the relevant work and can talk about it specifically. Ask if they're free before you type their email into a system that will contact them. Then send the program link, your project, your current materials, what the program wants them to cover, and the deadline with its time zone.

Give them time, and send one reminder if you need to. If the portal shows whether a letter arrived, check it. Sending the request doesn't mean the letter is in.

## How many residencies should I apply to at once?

Apply to as many good-fit programs as you can prepare properly with the time and money you have.

There's no proven right number. A handful of well-chosen programs can share core materials, but each still needs its own proposal, sample selection and eligibility check.

Here's a working schedule for one deadline. It's our advice, not any organizer's rule:

1. **Four weeks before:** check eligibility, funding and whether you could actually go. You want a shortlist you'd accept if selected.
2. **Three weeks before:** choose samples and ask for any required references. Finish with a complete materials folder.
3. **Two weeks before:** draft the proposal and fit it to this program.
4. **One week before:** check files, links, budget and requirements against the rules.
5. **A few days before:** submit and save the receipt.

Start earlier if passports, permissions or collaborators are involved, and leave room to fix an upload problem without counting on an extension. Save each residency call on Missa and you'll get reminders two weeks, one week, three days and one day before the deadline, in your time zone.

## What does a residency cost, and which ones pay you?

Count three costs separately: applying, attending, and what you'll spend yourself. Then set any stipend or grant against them.

Housing and a studio don't cover everything. Ask about meals, travel, materials, insurance, local transport and the rent you'll keep paying at home, and whether support arrives before you travel or after you've paid. The programs in the table show the range:

- MacDowell charges no residency fee and offers need-based stipends of [up to US$1,500](https://www.macdowell.org/apply/financial-assistance), plus travel reimbursement grants.
- Skowhegan charges US$6,000 tuition, but it's need-blind and says no accepted artist is turned away for lack of funding.
- The Albee Foundation charges nothing to apply or stay. Domestic fellows get a US$2,500 stipend and international fellows can claim expenses up to US$2,500, both paid after the residency.
- Jan van Eyck pays €1,500 a month, takes the rent out of it, and charges a €2,750 enrollment fee.
- PLOP's free studio space doesn't come with housing.

Those differences decide whether you can say yes to an offer, even when the application itself is cheap.

Our [guide to residencies with no application fee](/guides/free-artist-residencies) has a full cost checklist, and the [Nigeria and Africa funding guide](/guides/fully-funded-opportunities-nigeria-africa) covers residence rules and travel. To compare programs, look them up in the [Missa directory](/directory) or browse [residencies with no application fee](/discover/residencies-no-fee).

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I apply without a long exhibition or publication history?

Yes, at some programs. Check each one's actual career-stage rules and send strong eligible samples, instead of ruling yourself out because of a program's reputation.

### Can I reuse a proposal?

Partly. Reuse your project's facts and core materials, then explain why this residency suits the work. Check every word limit and required document again.

### Are all residencies free to attend?

No. Some charge tuition or participation costs, and others cover set costs or offer financial aid. Free to apply and funded to attend are separate questions.

### Do I apply through Missa?

No. Each call on Missa links to the organizer's page, and you apply there.

meta.title: Literary magazine acceptance rates, and what they don’t tell you
meta.seoTitle: Literary Magazine Acceptance Rates: What the Numbers Mean
meta.description: Where literary magazine acceptance rates come from, what’s known about The Paris Review and other top magazines, and how to build a sensible submission list.
meta.summary: Where acceptance-rate numbers come from, what they say about The Paris Review and others, and how to use them without reading too much in.
secondaryKeywords: how hard is it to get into the paris review
meta.answer: Most literary magazine acceptance rates come from writers’ own reports to trackers like Duotrope and Chill Subs, not from the magazines. They describe that sample, not your chances. The Paris Review gives no acceptance rate in its guidelines. Read any number with its source and date, then weigh fit, reading periods and response times.
keyPoints: Most acceptance rates are tracker figures from writers’ own reports, not official magazine numbers.
Duotrope’s 0.00% for The Paris Review means no acceptance reports in its sample.
Official response times we checked run from two months to a year.
