literary-magazine-acceptance-rates.body:
> [!NOTE]
> Every rate below comes from Duotrope or Chill Subs, mostly from their users’ own reports, and carries the date we saw it. Missa doesn’t publish acceptance rates. Tracker figures are snapshots and may mix genres.

## What’s The Paris Review’s acceptance rate?

The Paris Review doesn’t give an acceptance rate in its public guidelines, so any number you see comes from someone else’s sample.

Trackers can show a number that looks precise without describing the whole pool. On [Duotrope’s Paris Review page](https://duotrope.com/magazine/the-paris-review-133), the snapshot compiled October 1, 2026 showed 0.00% accepted. Duotrope says plainly what that means: it hasn’t received any acceptance reports for that sample. It doesn’t mean the magazine accepts nobody.

The [Paris Review’s own guidelines](https://www.theparisreview.org/about/submissions) say it reads unsolicited work, give examples of what it has published, and put the average wait at three to six months. That’s a far better basis for deciding than a reported zero.

Looking for the Paris Review poetry acceptance rate in particular? Don’t use an all-genre tracker figure. You’d need a poetry-only sample, its date, how many submissions it counts and what it leaves out. Without those, a precise percentage claims more than the source knows.

## Where do acceptance-rate numbers come from?

A reported acceptance rate is worked out from whatever records the reporting service has, which usually means its own users’ reports.

Duotrope’s [statistics page](https://duotrope.com/about/statistics.aspx) explains what its user reports can and can’t show. Chill Subs’ [listing guide](https://support.chillsubs.com/how-tos/how-to-navigate-our-listing-pages) marks community-sourced figures with an asterisk and has an “Editor’s Report” section for figures it labels official. Read both explanations before you compare their numbers.

Plenty can change a percentage:

- A tracker might count submissions, pieces or writers.
- A packet of poems might count as one submission, even if only one poem is taken.
- One writer can add many records.
- Pending work, withdrawals and no-replies may be counted differently from decisions.

The people who use trackers aren’t the whole pool, either. Writers who keep detailed records may submit differently from writers who don’t. Some users report acceptances more faithfully than rejections, or stop updating altogether. So the data describes the sample, not everyone who sent work.

An official rate needs a clear top and bottom number too. “We receive this many poems” doesn’t tell you how many submissions came in, how many were eligible or how many published poems were solicited. Don’t divide one kind of count by another and call it an acceptance rate.

## What do reported rates look like at top magazines?

Where Chill Subs showed a rate for the magazines below, it ran from 0.76% to 2.41% on October 7, 2026. Duotrope’s Paris Review sample showed 0.00%, because it had no acceptance reports.

“None found” means we didn’t find a current figure we could compare. It isn’t a zero. Where Chill Subs shows two values split by a slash, we’ve copied them as shown; the two can mean different things.

| Magazine | Reported acceptance rate | Source and date | Response time | Reading period |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The Paris Review | 0.00%, with Duotrope’s note: no acceptance reports | [Duotrope](https://duotrope.com/magazine/the-paris-review-133), compiled Oct 1, seen Oct 7, 2026 | Three to six months (official) | Separate online windows for prose and poetry; caps apply ([guidelines](https://www.theparisreview.org/about/submissions)) |
| A Public Space | 0.76% (not an official rate) | [Chill Subs](https://www.chillsubs.com/magazine/a-public-space), Oct 7, 2026 | Chill Subs shows “93 days/120 days after deadline” | Several reading periods ([official](https://apublicspace.org/about/resources)) |
| The Kenyon Review | 2.41% (not an official rate) | [Chill Subs](https://www.chillsubs.com/magazine/kenyon-review), Oct 7, 2026 | Within six months (official) | September 1–30, 2026, now closed ([guidelines](https://kenyonreview.org/submit/)) |
| AGNI | 0.92% (not an official rate) | [Chill Subs](https://www.chillsubs.com/magazine/agni), Oct 7, 2026 | Two to four months online (official) | September 1–December 15 and January 15–May 31 ([guidelines](https://agnionline.bu.edu/submit/)) |
| Brevity | “1.49%/2%”; check which value is which | [Chill Subs](https://www.chillsubs.com/magazine/brevity), Oct 7, 2026 | Chill Subs shows “62 days/60 days” | Check the live form ([guidelines](https://brevitymag.com/submissions/)) |
| Poetry | None found | [Official page](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/submit), Oct 7, 2026 | Up to one year (official) | Closed June 15–September 15 each year |
| One Story | None found | [Official guidelines](https://one-story.com/write/submit-a-story/), Oct 7, 2026 | None found | Closed when we checked; reopening announced for early December 2026 |
| Ploughshares | None found | [Official page](https://pshares.org/product/manuscript-submission/), Oct 7, 2026 | None found; check before you query | June 1–November 15; the contest is separate |

Read these as examples of how to read a source, not as a selectivity ranking. An unknown sample size or a mixed-genre pool matters more than the second decimal place.

## What’s a normal acceptance rate for a literary magazine?

There isn’t one. No single rate tells you whether a magazine is a good place for your work.

Magazines differ in format, space, how much they receive and what they’re for. A journal that publishes one long story has less room than one that runs many short poems. A themed call draws a different crowd from a general reading period. A new magazine may have too few reports for any comparison at all.

A better question: does this magazine publish the kind of work I’ve finished, and do I want its readers to find it? Read recent issues. Look at length, form, voice and how the pieces move, not only what they’re about. Notice what you share with them, but don’t imitate.

Then check the practical side: who can submit, the fee, simultaneous submissions, rights and the reading period. A moderately selective magazine that bans simultaneous submissions can hold a piece longer than a very selective one that allows them. Let your time and your goals decide.

## How long do top magazines take to respond?

Two months to a year, going by the official guidance in the table: AGNI says two to four months for online submissions, The Paris Review three to six months, The Kenyon Review within six months, and Poetry up to a year.

Those are stated expectations, not promises. Workload, submission caps and category can all change one writer’s wait.

When you send a piece, note the date and the magazine’s rule on queries. If it says to wait a set time, put a check-in date at the end of it. Don’t query early because another writer got a fast rejection.

Tracker averages need care. A mean gets pulled up by a few very long waits. A median is the middle result. Neither tells you that a piece still out past that date is more likely to be taken.

Before you chase anything, check your spam folder and your submission account. If you do write to the magazine, include the title, category, date sent and any reference number. Follow the magazine’s own query policy over a directory’s general advice.

## Should you still submit to magazines that accept under 1%?

Yes, if the work fits and you’re fine with the rules, the cost and the wait.

A low reported rate is a reason to send to more places, not a verdict on your work. Read the magazine before you decide either way. And a famous name isn’t a reason to send work outside its scope.

Don’t turn a percentage into a forecast. Your piece isn’t a random draw from the tracker’s sample, and editors’ decisions aren’t repeated coin tosses. Sending a piece out many times doesn’t add up to an acceptance at some predictable point.

## How do you build a submission list across tiers?

Start with fit, then use reputation and the practical rules to decide the order.

Pick magazines you’d read even if you weren’t submitting. Group them by what matters to you: a wide readership, strong work in your form, a particular community, contributor pay or an easy submission process. Our [guide to literary magazine tiers](/guides/best-literary-magazines-to-submit-to) goes through those groups.

For each magazine, note:

- [ ] Genre and length limit
- [ ] When it’s open
- [ ] The fee, if any
- [ ] Rights it asks for
- [ ] Response time and its rule on queries
- [ ] Whether it allows simultaneous submissions

Then pick a first group you can manage, with some ambitious picks, some long-standing journals that fit well and some smaller magazines you love. If simultaneous submissions are allowed, keep a record of everywhere the piece is and withdraw quickly when it’s taken.

Decide how much you’ll send, and keep making and revising new work while it’s out, so one magazine never decides what you do next. Some writers aim for 100 rejections a year. Pick your number.

For research, start with Missa’s [journal profiles](/journals) and the [magazine rankings](/rankings/magazines), which score reply time and simultaneous-submission policy among six measures. Then check the response time and rules on the magazine’s own page before you send. If you want a statistics database, our [Duotrope alternatives guide](/guides/duotrope-alternatives) compares the options.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does a 0% acceptance rate mean a magazine takes nothing?

No. It usually means the tracker has no acceptance reports in that sample. Read the source’s note and the magazine’s own guidelines.

### Is there an official Paris Review poetry acceptance rate?

Not one we could find. Its guidelines don’t give one, and an all-genre figure from tracker users isn’t a poetry rate.

### Does a long wait mean the editors like my work?

Not on its own. Follow the magazine’s response and query guidance, and keep the piece marked pending until you hear.

### Does Missa publish acceptance rates?

No. Missa’s magazine rankings score six measures, including pay and reply time, and acceptance rates aren’t one of them. For a reported rate, check Duotrope or Chill Subs and note the date.

meta.title: Submission fees and tip jars: when it’s worth paying to submit
meta.seoTitle: Literary Magazine Submission Fees and Tip Jars: When to Pay
meta.description: Why some literary magazines charge reading fees, when a contest fee is fair, what an optional tip jar really is, and how to find magazines that read for free.
meta.summary: Reading fees, contest fees and tip jars: what each one buys, when to pay, and how to find magazines that read for free.
meta.answer: A submission fee pays for your work to be read, not accepted. An optional tip jar should let you submit without paying. Pay only when the magazine fits your work, the terms are clear and the fee fits your budget. Free reading periods, fee waivers and no-fee magazines keep regular submitting affordable.
keyPoints: A reading fee pays for consideration. It doesn’t buy a better chance of acceptance.
A tip jar is only optional if the same submission goes through without paying.
Set a yearly limit you can afford without an acceptance, and log every fee.
meta.illustrationAlt: Illustration separating a required reading fee from an optional donation.

literary-magazine-submission-fees.body:
## Why do literary magazines charge submission fees?

Magazines charge to help pay for reading, admin and publishing, but only the magazine itself can tell you what its fee pays for.

[AGNI’s guidelines](https://agnionline.bu.edu/submit/) say its US$3 online reading fee helps pay the editors who read your work. AGNI also offers fee waivers, and work sent on paper costs nothing to submit. That’s AGNI’s reason. Don’t assume it applies to every magazine with an online form.

A free account and a free submission are two different things. The submission manager may let you sign up for free while the magazine charges for a particular category. Look at the actual form, including any required add-ons, before you confirm.

A published reason makes a fee easier to judge. It doesn’t mean you have to pay it. You can read and support a magazine without paying every reading fee it offers.

## Is it normal to pay to submit to a literary magazine?

Some magazines charge reading fees, but many read general submissions for free, and you never have to use a paid route.

[The Kenyon Review](https://kenyonreview.org/submit/) says it doesn’t charge a reading fee for general submissions. [Poetry](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/submit) says submitting is free. Neither means every contest or special category elsewhere is free.

Duotrope’s [fee advice for editors](https://duotrope.com/duosuma/docs/fee-recommendations.aspx) says the most common fee among the few journals that charge one is US$3, and that anything from US$2 to US$5 is in the average range. That’s Duotrope’s reading of its own listings, not an industry standard or a judgment of value.

Start by working out what kind of payment you’re looking at. “Varies” means we couldn’t find a reliable general range.

| Fee type | Typical amount | What it should get you | Fair when | Think twice when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| General reading fee | Varies; [AGNI](https://agnionline.bu.edu/submit/) charges US$3 online | Consideration under published rules | The magazine fits and the terms are clear | It’s presented as a way to get accepted |
| Expedited response | Varies | A faster reply in a stated timeframe | You have a real scheduling need | It implies better treatment, or refunds are unclear |
| Optional tip jar | Your choice, including nothing | The standard submission, without donating | You want to support the magazine | There’s no working way to submit for free |
| Contest entry | Varies by contest | Entry into a defined competition | Prize, judge, eligibility, rights and dates are clear | The prize or later costs are unclear |
| Free reading period | US$0 during that window | Standard consideration | The window is open for your category | A payment shows up before you finish |

## When is a contest entry fee fair?

A contest fee is easiest to judge when the organizer publishes the prize, how it’s judged, who can enter, the rights and the full cost before you pay.

Read the contest rules on their own, apart from the magazine’s regular guidelines. Check what work qualifies, how finalists are picked, what happens if the contest is canceled and whether the winner is guaranteed publication. Find out about any required book purchase or later charge.

Judge a prize on terms you can check. A big advertised award isn’t enough if the eligibility rules leave you out or the rights terms don’t work for you. The work should fit the category, not be squeezed in because the prize looks good.

Compare the contest with sending the same work to no-fee magazines, where that’s allowed. If what you want is publication, not the prize itself, that alternative matters. If you do enter, log the fee, currency, deadline and contract terms with the submission.

Browse [free contests](/discover/free-contests) for alternatives, and check [chapbook contests](/discover/chapbook-contests) for manuscript rules. A book-length contest has different preparation and publication terms from a single-poem competition.

## What’s a tip jar, and is it really optional?

A tip jar is an optional donation. If you can’t submit without paying, it’s a fee, whatever it’s called.

Check the form for a working way to submit the same category without donating. Read what the magazine says about reading order, response times and how submissions are treated. A separate paid service should be labeled as one, not tucked inside the tip jar.

If the form isn’t clear, ask the magazine whether you can submit without paying and how. Don’t pay first and count on a refund. Save their answer or the instructions for next time.

A donation should be its own decision about supporting the magazine. You shouldn’t have to guess whether donating helps your result. If a magazine says tips change how work is read, treat that as a paid service and decide whether you want it.

Missa’s “No fee” and “Fee not listed” labels separate a stated fee from missing information. Still check the form itself: a listing can’t cover every add-on or category.

## How do I find magazines that read for free?

Start with no-fee listings, then check the magazine’s current categories and reading window on its own site.

Open [magazine calls](/discover/magazines) and sort by “Free to apply first,” or start from [no-fee calls](/discover/no-fee-calls) and pick out the magazines. Check that the magazine takes your genre and that the no-fee statement covers the exact category you’re sending.

Some magazines have free periods at certain times, waivers on request or free entry for subscribers. A subscription still costs money, so treat it as buying something to read that comes with a submission perk. It isn’t free for anyone who doesn’t already subscribe.

Mail can have no reading fee and still cost you printing and postage. Compare that total with the online fee, especially if you’re mailing internationally. Check that the magazine accepts paper submissions before you send anything.

> [!TIP]
> When a free window has closed, put the next one in your calendar and have the work ready before it opens. You won’t have to rush the final draft.

## How much should I budget for submissions in a year?

Set a limit you can afford without a single acceptance, and log every fee as you pay it.

Here’s a made-up budget, not an average writer’s spending. Twenty general submissions at US$3 each come to US$60. Two contests at US$20 each add US$40. That’s US$100 in fees before subscriptions, postage or anything else. Small fees add up.

Pick a yearly or quarterly limit, then split it across the things you actually value. A tracker subscription and a submission fee are separate costs. Give tips and workshops their own lines too, so they don’t vanish into a general writing budget.

Look back at your spending now and then. Note which fees didn’t lead to a useful experience and decide whether to repeat them. A rejection doesn’t make a fee unfair. A hidden charge or a service that never arrived is a different problem.

If your budget is zero, build your list from confirmed free routes. You can still make a long list without treating every familiar magazine as a must-pay.

## What should I check before paying?

Check four things before you pay: the fit, the full charge, the submission terms and where the money is going.

- [ ] Read recent work in the magazine
- [ ] Check the genre and length limits
- [ ] Check whether it’s a regular submission or a contest
- [ ] Read the rights and simultaneous-submission policy
- [ ] Check the final amount and currency at checkout
- [ ] Confirm who you’re paying
- [ ] Keep the receipt

If you’re not sure who the organizer is or where the payment is going, use the [scam-check guide](/guides/open-call-scams-vanity-galleries). For exhibition costs, the [guide to entry and participation fees](/guides/entry-fees-hanging-fees-participation-fees) separates what you pay before and after selection.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does a submission fee improve my chance of acceptance?

Not by itself. A standard fee pays for the consideration the rules describe. It doesn’t guarantee editorial interest or acceptance.

### Is an optional tip jar a no-fee submission?

Yes, if you can finish the submission without donating. Check the actual form and category.

### Are fee waivers available?

Some magazines offer them. AGNI does, on request. Follow each magazine’s own process before you pay.

open-call-scams-vanity-galleries.body:
## How can I tell if an open call is a scam?

A scam lies about an offer, or about who’s behind it, to get your money, your information or something else. A fee on its own doesn’t make a call a scam.

Look for facts you can check yourself. Does the venue confirm the show? Can you find out who’s organizing it and who’s choosing the work? Are the application and post-selection costs both disclosed? Do the promised services come with dates and specifics?

Some offers are plain impersonation. [White Cube’s security guidance](https://www.whitecube.com/cyber-security-guidance) says it doesn’t charge fees for exhibitions or for reviewing work, and tells artists to check unexpected approaches through its own contact page. A paid invitation in White Cube’s name contradicts that published policy.

The [Royal Academy’s Summer Exhibition site](https://summer.royalacademy.org.uk/Home/) also warns that scammers are sending artists personal invitations to submit. A familiar logo and a real exhibition name don’t prove the sender represents the institution.

## What’s a vanity gallery?

A vanity gallery sells exhibition places to artists, often presenting the payment as a mark of selection or prestige.

The term describes a business model and a worry about value. It doesn’t prove that every service on offer is fraudulent. The useful questions are what you’re buying, whether selection means anything and whether the claims match the actual service.

A rented venue, an artist cooperative or a clearly priced group show can also charge artists. Judge those by their terms and purpose. A cooperative’s membership is a different thing from an unsolicited message implying a commercial gallery wants to represent you, followed by a request for money.

Ask whether the organizer earns mostly from selling places to artists, and how it shows that artists get what they’re promised. A photo of a busy opening doesn’t prove sales or lasting interest. Treat claims about collectors, curators and career boosts as questions that need evidence.

Our [guide to entry, hanging and participation fees](/guides/entry-fees-hanging-fees-participation-fees) explains the cost labels before you weigh up an offer.

## Is an unsolicited invitation to exhibit a red flag?

Not always, but it’s a reason to check carefully, especially when it asks for money, personal details or high-resolution files.

Look at the sender’s address and the reply-to address, then find the organizer’s official website yourself. A small spelling change in a domain is enough to impersonate someone. Real staff names get copied too, so finding that person on the website doesn’t prove the email came from them.

Then contact the organization through its own site and ask whether the invitation is real. Include the sender’s address and the key details, without unnecessary attachments. Don’t call a number that only appears in the suspicious message.

Specific claims should be checkable. An organizer who says they saw your work should be able to name it and say why it suits the show. Generic praise doesn’t prove dishonesty, but it gives you little reason to spend money.

> [!WARNING]
> Pressure to pay fast is the clearest red flag: a short payment deadline, a warning that you’ll lose your place, or a request to keep the invitation to yourself. Don’t pay until you’ve checked with the organization through its own website.

## Is it ever fine to pay to exhibit?

Sometimes. Paying for a defined exhibition service is reasonable when you know the full cost, the terms and what it’s worth to you.

Decide what you’re buying: a specific room, help with installation, a public event or another concrete service. Compare the price with other ways to get the same thing. Find out what happens if the show changes or is canceled.

Don’t pay for a vague promise of reputation. A venue in a well-known city doesn’t guarantee the right audience, press attention or future representation. Ask about opening hours, access, promotion and past shows. If sales matter to you, check the commission, how sales are handled and when you’re paid.

A disappointing show and a fraudulent one are different problems. You can turn down a poor-value offer without proving it’s a scam. Price is only one part of the check.

## How do I check an organizer before I pay?

Spend ten minutes checking the venue, the people, past shows, every fee and the terms, using sources other than the invitation itself.

Ten minutes won’t settle everything. If something important is still unclear, hold off on paying and keep looking.

| Check | Where to look | Good sign | Red flag |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Venue and dates | The venue’s own program or contact page | The venue confirms the show and schedule | A vague “international gallery” with no named location |
| Organizer and jurors | Official site, staff pages, independent professional pages | Named people and a described selection process | An affiliation the institution won’t confirm |
| Past exhibitions | Archived programs and past artists’ own accounts | Consistent evidence the named shows happened | Images with no context, or claims past artists dispute |
| Every required fee | The call, application form and agreement | All costs disclosed before you apply | A new required package after “acceptance” |
| Sales commission | The written sales terms | A clear calculation and payment arrangement | Nobody can explain what you’ll actually receive |
| Rights and image use | Entry rules and the proposed contract | Permissions tied to this exhibition | Broad rights with no clear purpose or end date |
| Shipping and insurance | Delivery terms and the organizer’s written answer | Responsibility, return route and cover are clear | No return plan, or unclear damage liability |
| Other artists’ experience | Independent accounts and direct questions | Specific descriptions of what was delivered | Repeated, documented problems with the service |

Keep what you found separate from what you think. “The venue confirmed the booking” is a fact. “This seems worth my budget” is your decision. One good comment online shouldn’t outweigh an open question about payment or rights.

For a general check, use [how to check a call before you apply](/guides/verify-an-opportunity-before-applying). It covers current rules and where to apply. This guide is about identity, payment and misleading invitations.

## Does a Missa listing mean a call is safe?

Not on its own. A Missa listing links to the organizer’s page and marks what we couldn’t confirm, but it doesn’t guarantee you’re eligible or that the organizer will deliver.

You apply on the organizer’s page, not through Missa. The [methodology](/methodology) explains how calls are checked: the fee, dates and rules are each checked and shown on their own, and if two sources disagree, the listing says so. Read the organizer’s page before you apply. If the page doesn’t say, neither do we.

A listing isn’t a recommendation to pay. If one looks wrong, report it through the methodology page so it can be fixed. A current deadline and a clear application link are useful, but they can’t tell you whether a show is worth it for your work.

[No-fee calls](/discover/no-fee-calls) can cut what you spend on applications, but a free application isn’t a certificate of trust. Writers should also check the costs and terms in our [submission-fee guide](/guides/literary-magazine-submission-fees).

## What should I do if I’ve already paid?

Save the evidence and contact your bank, card issuer or payment service quickly if you think you paid a scammer.

1. **Save everything.** Keep the call, the agreement, the invoice, the receipt, the messages and where the payment went.
2. **Contact whoever handled the payment.** The US Federal Trade Commission’s [guide for people who’ve been scammed](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/what-do-if-you-were-scammed) sets out what to do for each payment method. What’s possible depends on how you paid and where you live, and getting the money back isn’t guaranteed.
3. **Ask the organizer in writing** about any service or refund you were promised and didn’t get. Keep it factual.
4. **Report impersonation.** If someone pretended to be a gallery or institution, tell that organization through its official contact details. You can also report it to your country’s fraud-reporting service. In the US, the FTC takes reports through [ReportFraud](https://reportfraud.ftc.gov/).

Be wary of anyone who offers to get your money back for an upfront fee. The FTC’s [refund and recovery scam guidance](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/refund-and-recovery-scams) says never to pay upfront for help getting a refund. Check any recovery service independently before you share information or pay again.

## Frequently asked questions

### Are all paid art competitions scams?

No. A fee can be part of a disclosed selection process. Check the organizer, the full terms and the value, not just the price.

### Does an exhibition in New York or London guarantee useful exposure?

No. Check the venue, the audience and the services. A city name doesn’t tell you who’ll come or what the organizer will deliver.

### Is an unnamed jury proof of a scam?

No, but it’s missing information. Check whether the selection process is explained, and ask the organizer before you pay.

### Can a call without a fee still be unsafe?

Yes. Identity, rights, requests for personal data and delivery terms still matter. Free entry doesn’t settle any of them.

where-to-find-open-calls.body:
An open call is any invitation to send work or apply under stated rules. The real question is where to find the ones that fit what you make, where you live and what you can spend.

> [!NOTE]
> Missa publishes this guide and is one of the ten sites compared. The order isn't a ranking, and Missa's entry lists its limits like the others.

## What's the best site to find open calls?

The best one depends on what you make and what you need from it: a list of calls, a place to apply, or a record of what you sent.

Pick a starting point from the table, then read the notes below it. "Not stated on their site" means we couldn't find it on their public pages, not that the feature doesn't exist. Prices are what the site charges you, separate from any fee the organizer charges.

| Site | Best for | Price for you | Fee on the listing | No-fee filter | Deadline reminders | Submission tracking |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [ArtConnect](https://www.artconnect.com/opportunities/opencalls?types=OPEN_CALL) | Visual art calls and residencies, international | [Free: 5 calls a month. Paid: $3–$10 a month](https://artconnect.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/7886405974802-What-membership-plans-are-available-for-artists-and-curators) | "Free" or "Yes" tag, no amount | [Page of calls without fees](https://www.artconnect.com/opportunities/without-fees) | Paid plans add deadlines to your calendar | Not stated on their site |
| [CuratorSpace](https://www.curatorspace.com/support/faqs) | Exhibition calls with the application built in | Free for artists; upgrades from £5 a month | On each call's page, not the list | Not stated on their site | [Emails for bookmarked calls](https://www.curatorspace.com/opportunities) | Status of applications made there |
| [CaFÉ](https://www.callforentry.org/) | Juried exhibitions and public art; US regions plus outside the US | [Free account](https://artist-help.callforentry.org/doc/my-creative-west-account) | [Application fee on each card](https://opportunities.wearecreativewest.org/) | [Set the fee range to $0](https://artist-help.callforentry.org/doc/searching-for-opportunities) | [Opt-in emails for calls you follow](https://artist-help.callforentry.org/doc/opportunities-portal-faqs) | My Entries, for CaFÉ applications |
| [NYFA](https://www.nyfa.org/opportunities/) | Grants, residencies and calls across art forms | [Free account](https://www.nyfa.org/news/nyfa-classifieds-now-offers-account-creation-unlocking-personalized-recommendations-for-listings-and-professional-development/) | Not stated on their site | "No Fee Application" filter | Not stated on their site | Saved listings plus an applications snapshot |
| [Artenda](https://artenda.net/) | International visual art calls and residencies | 30 days free, then €3.49 a month | Application fee and rent/fee fields | Not stated on their site | [Emails for calls in your agenda](https://artenda.net/en/faq) | Not stated on their site |
| [ArtRabbit](https://www.artrabbit.com/artist-opportunities) | A curated pick of art calls, next to exhibition listings | Free to browse | Entry fee in some listings | Not stated on their site | Not stated on their site | Not stated on their site |
| [Submittable Discover](https://submittable.help/en/articles/7940128-getting-started-as-a-new-submitter) | Calls that take work through Submittable forms | [Free account](https://submittable.help/en/articles/904856-how-can-i-submit) | [On the call's details page](https://submittable.help/en/articles/904853-how-can-i-find-and-follow-opportunities-on-submittable) | "No Fee" filter | [Unfinished drafts only; saved calls not listed](https://submittable.help/en/articles/4926006-what-notifications-should-i-expect-to-receive-from-submittable-as-a-submitter) | Status, plus manual records of outside submissions |
| [Poets & Writers](https://www.pw.org/literary_magazines) | Researching literary magazines | [Free to search; free account to save](https://www.pw.org/literary_magazines/32_poems) | Says if there's a reading fee, not the amount | "Reading Fee: No" filter | Not stated on their site | Not stated on their site |
| [Chill Subs](https://support.chillsubs.com/how-tos/how-to-use-our-submission-tracker) | Literary magazines, contests and presses | [Basic tracking free; Better US$10 a month](https://support.chillsubs.com/faq/memberships) | [Exact fee on each call](https://support.chillsubs.com/how-tos/how-to-navigate-our-listing-pages) | ["No fee" filter](https://support.chillsubs.com/how-tos/how-to-use-saved-search) | Not stated on their site | Tracker with CSV import and export |
| [Missa](/methodology) | Calls across art, writing, film, music and performance | Finding, saving and email reminders free | Fee, "No fee" or "Fee not listed" | [No-fee calls page](/discover/no-fee-calls) | Two weeks, one week, three days and one day before | What you sent, where and when; [CSV import](/import) |

## Which open call websites should visual artists try?

Try ArtConnect for range, CuratorSpace or CaFÉ when you want to apply on the same site, NYFA for grants across art forms, Artenda for reminders and ArtRabbit for an edited weekly pick. Pick by the kind of application you're making, not by how many calls a site says it has.

### ArtConnect

ArtConnect's [open call pages](https://www.artconnect.com/opportunities/opencalls?types=OPEN_CALL) put the deadline and a fee tag on every card, so you can tell a free call from one that charges before you click. There's also a page of [calls without fees](https://www.artconnect.com/opportunities/without-fees). Residencies, exhibitions, grants and commissions share one list, which helps if you're not after one kind of thing.

The tag says "Free" or "Yes", not how much. It won't cover shipping, travel or what you pay to take part, either. Read the organizer's rules and check you're eligible before you put time into an application.

The [free plan](https://artconnect.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/7886405974802-What-membership-plans-are-available-for-artists-and-curators) lets you view five calls a month. Emerging ($3 a month billed yearly, or $6 monthly) adds unlimited calls, a weekly email of matches, a saved list and a way to add deadlines to your calendar. Mid-career ($5 or $10) adds a full artist profile. The [pricing page](https://www.artconnect.com/memberships/artists) says prices don't include VAT.

### CuratorSpace

Use CuratorSpace when you'd like the call and the application in one place. Its [artist FAQ](https://www.curatorspace.com/support/faqs) says you can apply on the site, save an application to finish later and check its status in your account. That suits you if you're preparing several exhibition applications with images and supporting text. It's free for artists, with paid upgrades from £5 a month.

Bookmark a call and they'll [send reminders](https://www.curatorspace.com/opportunities) as the deadline gets close or if the details change. Each call's cost is on its own page, not in the list. The free account doesn't make the call free: organizers can still charge an entry or exhibition fee. And the status page only covers what you sent through CuratorSpace, so keep a record of email submissions somewhere else.

### CaFÉ and Creative West

If an organizer asks you to upload images, answer eligibility questions or enter work for a jury on CaFÉ, start there. It's built for juried exhibitions and public art, and your applications, started and sent, sit on a [My Entries page](https://artist-help.callforentry.org/doc/opportunities-portal-faqs).

Its "Find Calls" link now opens [a Creative West portal](https://opportunities.wearecreativewest.org/), the new version of the CaFÉ call listings, so older screenshots of the filters won't match. Each card shows the application fee. For free calls, [set the fee range to zero](https://artist-help.callforentry.org/doc/searching-for-opportunities); there's also a "$25 and Under" shortcut. Earlier [product updates](https://www.callforentry.org/administrator-help-center/cafe-product-updates/) added a filter for participation fees collected through CaFÉ and an "Outside the US" region. Follow a call and, if you opt in, you'll get an email before it closes. The [account is free](https://artist-help.callforentry.org/doc/my-creative-west-account).

Check the practical fit, too. A regional show may need the work delivered in person, even though anyone can fill in the online form.

### NYFA

If your work crosses forms, [NYFA's board](https://www.nyfa.org/opportunities/) is a good place to look. It covers literary, performing and visual arts, with grants and residencies next to calls to show work, and its "No Fee Application" filter clears out application charges in one go. A [free account](https://www.nyfa.org/news/nyfa-classifieds-now-offers-account-creation-unlocking-personalized-recommendations-for-listings-and-professional-development/) saves listings and searches and emails you when new matches are posted.

Treat each result as a lead. The funder's own rules decide whether it fits you: a call filed under literary arts can still be limited by where you live, your experience or the kind of project. A no-fee application can also lead to a paid workshop or residency, so read the participation terms too.

### Artenda

Artenda is built around reminders. Add a call to your agenda and they'll [email you before the deadline](https://artenda.net/en/faq). Its [listings](https://artenda.net/) show the application fee apart from the residency's rent or fee, which helps when your shortlist mixes supported residencies with programs that charge you to attend.

It's €3.49 a month after a 30-day free trial, and the subscription starts on its own unless you cancel. Check the checkout currency, the billing terms and what your account can search before you pay. The coverage is art calls, so if you're sending out poems or stories you'll still want a magazine database.

### ArtRabbit

ArtRabbit [picks its calls](https://www.artrabbit.com/artist-opportunities) from submissions and its own research, and emails a selection to about 23,500 art practitioners every week. You can filter by type and location, and some listings give the entry fee. The bonus is the exhibition listings on the same site: look up a venue's past shows and artists to see whether the call fits the work it actually shows. Their site doesn't mention a submission tracker or deadline reminders, so keep your own calendar and record.

## Where do writers find magazine calls and contests?

Research in a magazine database such as Poets & Writers or Chill Subs, find calls with a form attached on Submittable Discover, and get the final rules from the magazine's own submission page.

### Submittable Discover

Discover lists calls that take work through Submittable's own forms, so you go straight from the call to the form. You can [search by topic and date, save calls and follow organizations](https://submittable.help/en/articles/904853-how-can-i-find-and-follow-opportunities-on-submittable), and there's a ["No Fee" filter](https://submittable.help/en/articles/7940128-getting-started-as-a-new-submitter). The account is [free](https://submittable.help/en/articles/904856-how-can-i-submit).

Once you send something, it sits in your account with its status, and Submittable [emails you when the status changes](https://submittable.help/en/articles/4926006-what-notifications-should-i-expect-to-receive-from-submittable-as-a-submitter). Its notification list includes reminders for unfinished drafts, but not deadline reminders for saved calls. You can also [add submissions made elsewhere](https://submittable.help/en/articles/13380905-external-submissions) by hand, so the tracker isn't limited to Submittable. You enter those yourself, though; another magazine's email decision won't show up on its own. Before you send, check the form for genre, fee, any cap on submissions and the files it wants.

### Poets & Writers

The [Poets & Writers database](https://www.pw.org/literary_magazines) is for working out where your work belongs, not just which deadline is next. Filter by genre, payment, response time and whether a magazine is open now or opens within 30 days, and set "Reading Fee" to No to drop the ones that charge. Each [entry](https://www.pw.org/literary_magazines/32_poems) says whether there's a reading fee, though not how much, and the publishers supply the details themselves. A free account lets you save entries.

Use an entry as your way into the magazine's own site, where you can read the work and the current guidelines, including any language or residence rules. A magazine that's closed now can still go on your list for its next reading period. Contests run on their own terms: the fee, the prize and who can enter may differ from the usual reading period. Keep your own record of genre, manuscript, date sent, status and any withdrawal.

### Chill Subs

Got a submissions spreadsheet already? Chill Subs is worth a test. Its [tracker](https://support.chillsubs.com/how-tos/how-to-use-our-submission-tracker) imports a custom CSV or your Submittable and Submission Grinder exports, and exports back to CSV. Basic tracking is free for everyone. [Listing pages](https://support.chillsubs.com/how-tos/how-to-navigate-our-listing-pages) show each call's submission fee and the exact amount, Browse has a ["No fee" filter](https://support.chillsubs.com/how-tos/how-to-use-saved-search), and a [calendar](https://support.chillsubs.com/faq/using-chill-subs) shows upcoming deadlines.

The [membership FAQ](https://support.chillsubs.com/faq/memberships) lists Better at US$10 a month, separate from their newsletter and workshop subscriptions. The acceptance figures come from submissions writers report, not every manuscript a magazine gets, so check the sample size and labels before you trust a percentage. Our [Duotrope alternatives guide](/guides/duotrope-alternatives) compares trackers in more detail.

## Where does Missa fit in the comparison?

Missa lists calls across art, writing, film, music and performance, including residencies, grants and prizes, and keeps track of what you send.

Every call links to the organizer's page, and you apply there, not through Missa. Cards show the fee, "No fee", or "Fee not listed" when the organizer's page doesn't say. The [methodology](/methodology) explains how calls are checked. Save a call and you'll get an email two weeks, one week, three days and one day before the deadline, in your time zone. The tracker keeps what you sent, where and when, and you can [import your old spreadsheet](/import). Finding calls, saving them and email reminders are free.

It has limits. Missa doesn't publish acceptance rates, and a listing doesn't promise you're eligible or that the organizer's page won't change. Confirm the current rules on their page, and update your records when things move. If you're researching an organization, start with the [directory](/directory). If where you live is the first filter, try [calls by country](/countries).

## Which sites show the fee and remind you before a deadline?

Chill Subs, CaFÉ, Artenda and Missa put the fee amount on the listing, and CuratorSpace, CaFÉ, Artenda and Missa can email you before a saved call closes.

Seven of the ten have a no-fee filter or page: ArtConnect, CaFÉ, NYFA, Submittable, Poets & Writers, Chill Subs and [Missa](/discover/no-fee-calls). ArtConnect and Poets & Writers tell you whether there's a fee, not how much.

A fee filter builds the shortlist, and a reminder gets you to act on it. Neither tells you the full cost or whether you can apply. Status emails are a different feature, too: a site that tells you about a decision won't necessarily remind you about a deadline. Our [guide to entry, hanging and participation fees](/guides/entry-fees-hanging-fees-participation-fees) explains why "free to apply" needs a second cost check.

## Where do artists outside the US and UK find calls?

Start with the international listings on ArtConnect or Artenda, then check who can apply before you treat a call as open to you.

ArtConnect's dashboard [uses your location](https://artconnect.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/10891814141202-How-does-my-location-affect-the-recommendations-on-my-dashboard) to show calls for artists where you live plus calls open to international artists; its full list of calls skips that filter. CaFÉ's search has an "Outside the US" region, NYFA lets you narrow by location and discipline, and Missa has [calls by country](/countries). The venue's country isn't the country you have to live in. A Paris residency could take someone living in Lagos, while a local grant might only take residents of one city.

Check travel funding, visa support, how they'll pay you and whether a grant is paid in advance. If the organizer hasn't explained a restriction, ask them a specific question before you start the application. Our [guide to funded calls in Nigeria and Africa](/guides/fully-funded-opportunities-nigeria-africa) goes through that check in more detail.

## How do you use several sites without losing track?

Use as many sites as you like to find calls, and keep one record of what you sent. Otherwise it's forty open tabs and a color-coded spreadsheet that only made sense in March.

Give each call a row with:

- [ ] The organizer's official page
- [ ] Deadline and time zone
- [ ] Who can apply
- [ ] Application fee and any participation cost
- [ ] What you still need to prepare
- [ ] Once sent: the work's title, version, date and status
- [ ] A withdrawal, the day the work is accepted elsewhere

When the same call shows up on two sites, compare the organizer, the category and the official page before you start a second application. Set yourself a finish date ahead of the deadline, and save the last day for uploading and checking the receipt.

> [!TIP]
> Short on time? Start with [calls closing this week](/discover/closing-this-week), then drop anything you can't finish well before then.

## Frequently asked questions

### Are open call websites free?

Many are free to search or give you a free account, and some sell subscriptions. The organizer may still charge its own entry, participation or attendance fee, however you found the call.

### Does a no-fee filter mean an exhibition costs nothing?

No. It usually covers the application charge. Shipping, framing, insurance, travel, commission and participation costs need checking separately in the organizer's terms.

### Should I pay for an open call subscription?

Only when one feature clearly earns its place in your routine, such as coverage, statistics or reminders. Try the free tools first and set the cost against your submission budget.
